title: Drop the cream identity: variant A palette, no highlight, no pills
description:
oh-my-portal-ve5 put a terminal frame around the page but kept the §12 cream
identity on top of it, and the result read as the old blog with a bar bolted on.
The maintainer looked at it and said nothing had changed. Three things were
doing that:

1. the yellow highlight behind every h1 — the loudest element on the page, and
   from a different design
2. pastel tag pills — a fill and a radius are the least terminal thing available,

3. the chrome spanned 62rem over a 34rem column, so the right end of the status

title: Crawler surface: sitemap, robots.txt, favicon, SITE_URL gate
description:
The build emits `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`, markdown twins, `/index.json` and
five RSS feeds. It does not emit the one file every ordinary crawler asks for.

- **No `sitemap.xml`.** `@astrojs/sitemap` is not installed.
- **No `robots.txt`.** There is no `public/` directory in the repository at all.
  It should point at the sitemap and at `/llms.txt`.
- **No favicon**, so every page load takes a 404 on `/favicon.ico`.
- **`SITE_URL` fails open.** `astro.config.mjs:9` is
  `process.env.SITE_URL ?? 'https://example.com'`. A build without the variable
  does not fail — it ships a site whose every `<link rel="canonical">`, every
  `hreflang`, and every absolute URL in `llms.txt`, `/index.json` and the feeds
  names `example.com`. A page declaring a foreign domain canonical is worse than
  a page declaring none, and it is precisely the silent per-address failure
  `scripts/check-outputs.ts` was written to refuse.

The gate belongs with R10's other checks: the placeholder is legitimate for
`astro build` in this repository, so `check-outputs.ts` — which runs on the
built artifact — is where it must be caught, not in the config.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] `dist/sitemap-index.xml` (or `sitemap.xml`) exists after a build and lists every indexable address
- [x] Draft, `/search/` and 404 addresses are absent from the sitemap, matching their `noindex`
- [x] `robots.txt` is served, references the sitemap absolutely, and points at `/llms.txt`
- [x] A favicon is served and referenced from `<head>`
- [x] `check-outputs.ts` fails a build whose canonical host is the `example.com` placeholder
- [x] That gate is proved by a test, not by reading the code
close_reason: Hand-rolled /sitemap.xml and /robots.txt endpoints rather than @astrojs/sitemap, because the plugin cannot know about noindex; a light/dark favicon.svg; and check-outputs.ts now fails a build whose canonical is the example.com placeholder, with CHECK_PLACEHOLDER_HOST=allow as the documented escape hatch for a local build. test/head.test.ts asserts set equality between the sitemap and the indexable addresses of a real build, and proves the gate by running it against a build made without SITE_URL.

title: Design system: the mark, the tag palette, the one real number
description:
The maintainer named a reference they call beautiful — maxtokens.ai — after
rejecting the terminal frame and the stripped-back version. Read what actually
makes it work rather than copying it: a wordmark that is a visual pun on the
subject, pastel tag chips, a sans UI, one computed number per row, a filter row
with counts, and a lot of air.

The mistake it exposed: three iterations optimised for honest and minimal, and
the ask was **beautiful**. danluu.com is respected for its writing, not admired
for its design; asking for one and building the other was the error.

What landed, and why each is specific to this site rather than borrowed:

- **The mark is the name over the corpus split into coloured counts.** Identity
  and filter in one object. The numbers are article counts, so the row's shape is
  the shape of what the author writes about, and it changes on its own as the
  archive grows. maxtokens' chips carry token ids because that site is about
  tokens; ours carry a taxonomy because this one is about a body of work.
- **Colour means exactly one thing: a tag.** Six pastels, stable per tag across
  every page, so the colour becomes a second name. This restores what the very
  first §12 asked for — pastel labels — which an earlier pass deleted wholesale.
- **One sans, monospace only for machine-produced values.** The serif read as
  "old blog", which is the opposite of the brief.
- **One number per row: the exact byte length of the markdown twin**, from
  `articleMarkdown()` — the same string the build emits at `/posts/<slug>.md`,
  not an estimate. This is the honest version of the fabricated telemetry that
  every rejected mockup leaned on: the form of instrumentation, with a figure
  that is completely true. Kilobytes rather than tokens because a token count
  needs a tokenizer and remains a guess about whose.
- **Three zones per row** — when, what, how much — metadata gathered at the right
  edge, the writing alone in the middle.

The mark is a component taking the name from `data/author.yaml`, because §2 says
this repository is an engine and carries no site of its own. It renders the
synthetic name until a content repository supplies a real one.

Trap worth recording: a prop named `as` makes astro check stop seeing the
component's `Props` interface entirely — callers then fail with "Property does
not exist on type 'IntrinsicAttributes'" and the component's own destructuring
reports implicit `any`. Renaming the prop fixed it; no cast or annotation did.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] A tag renders the same colour on the front page, in a listing row and on an article
- [x] Every row shows the exact byte length of its markdown twin, computed from the same function the twin route uses
- [x] Body and headings are sans; monospace appears only on dates, sizes, paths and code

- [x] Rows collapse to a single column below the three-column width

title: Phase 2: agent publishing pipeline
description:
The agent writes content/posts/<slug>.md and pushes branch draft/<slug>. CI builds a preview on a closed host (basic-auth, noindex), the agent sends the link to Telegram, the maintainer reviews on a phone and says publish, the agent merges to main. A draft never reaches production.

title: Head: titles, Open Graph, Twitter cards
description:
`src/layouts/Base.astro` renders twelve lines of `<head>` and none of them tell a
social client, or a human reading a tab strip, whose site this is.

`<title>` is the bare page title (`Base.astro:48`), so the homepage is `Записи`
while its own `<h1>` says «Собираю свою цифровую жизнь», and `/search/`,
`/projects/`, `/about/` are indistinguishable from any site in existence. The
author's name is already in scope — `getAuthor()` at `Base.astro:33` feeds the
wordmark.

There is no `og:*` or `twitter:*` tag anywhere, so a link pasted into Telegram,
Slack or X unfurls as a bare URL. For a site that ships `Link: </llms.txt>` on
every response, having explained everything to agents and nothing to a person in
a chat window is a strange place to have landed.

Articles additionally have `date`, `updated`, `tags` and `author` on hand in
`Post.astro`, which is exactly what `article:published_time`,
`article:modified_time`, `article:tag` and `article:author` want.

Scope: `Base.astro` and the props `Post.astro` passes it. The image itself is
oh-my-portal-og-image.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] Every page's `<title>` carries the site name, and the separator and order are stated once in `Base.astro` with the reason
- [x] The homepage title agrees with its own `<h1>` rather than contradicting it
- [x] A tag page leads with the tag, not with the word «Тема»
- [x] `og:type`, `og:title`, `og:description`, `og:url`, `og:site_name`, `og:locale` and `og:image` render on every page
- [x] `twitter:card`, `twitter:title`, `twitter:description`, `twitter:image` render on every page
- [x] An article renders `article:published_time`, `article:modified_time` when updated, `article:tag` per tag and `article:author`
- [x] `<meta name="author">` renders from the content repository's author, and is absent rather than wrong when no content repository is mounted
- [x] A test asserts the tags exist in a real build for one article and one listing page
close_reason: Base.astro composes the title through src/seo.ts (page first, site last; the homepage inverts it) and renders og:*, twitter:*, article:*, meta author and theme-color. Post.astro passes the frontmatter dates, tags and the human/being distinction. test/seo.test.ts covers the composition, test/head.test.ts asserts the tags in a real build.

title: npm run dev does not show drafts
description:
`PREVIEW=1` is the flag that makes drafts visible (src/posts.ts), and no script
sets it. So the local dev server hides exactly the post being written, and the
only way to see a draft is the CI preview flow in §7 — a push, a build and a
deploy to look at a paragraph.

This is the piece the maintainer asked about when pointing at Astro's Jekyll
migration guide: Jekyll's `_drafts` are visible with `jekyll serve --drafts`, and
the local equivalent here is one word in package.json.

Two ways: `PREVIEW=1` in the `dev` script, so writing always shows drafts and
production never does; or a separate `dev:drafts`. The first is almost certainly
right — the dev server is where drafts are written, and the flag already cannot
leak into a production build because that runs a different script.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The dev server shows drafts without anyone setting an environment variable by hand

title: kind: note is declared and used nowhere
description:
`kind: article | note | page` is in the schema (§4), and `note` is inert: nothing
branches on it. `listPosts` excludes only `page`, so a note renders exactly like
an article — same listing row, same article layout.

Worse, the schema makes a short post expensive: `title` and `summary` are both
required, and `summary` is capped at 200 characters. Writing a three-sentence
note therefore costs a title, a one-sentence abstract of three sentences, and a
tag decision. That friction is aimed at exactly the posts meant to be cheap.

The maintainer wants both long articles and short notes. Decide:

- Does a note need a title? A dated note with no title is the usual shape, but
  the title feeds the listing, the feeds, /index.json and llms.txt — so removing
  it means those projections need a fallback, probably the first line.
- Does a note need a summary? It is one sentence and the note may be three.
- Does a note appear in the same listing as articles, in a separate stream, or
  interleaved with a different row treatment?
- Does a note get its own feed, so subscribers can take articles only?

Whatever is decided, it lands in §4 and in the schema together — a `kind` that
changes nothing is worse than no `kind`, because it looks like it does.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] §4 says what a note is, what it requires, and where it appears
- [ ] The schema makes required fields conditional on kind, or the decision to keep them is recorded with its reason
- [ ] The archive renders a note differently from an article, or the decision not to is recorded
- [ ] The feeds, /index.json and llms.txt handle a note without a title if that is what was decided
- [ ] examples/posts carries one note

title: nginx example served the whole site as octet-stream, and markdown without a charset
description:
Two faults in `nginx/site.conf.example`, found because the maintainer opened a
`.md` twin in a browser and got mojibake. Both were verified against a real
nginx 1.30.4 rather than reasoned about, and both are fixed.

**1. `types` inside `server` replaced the MIME map instead of extending it.**

    types { text/markdown md; }

A `types` block in a nested context does not add to the map inherited from
`include mime.types` — it replaces it. Measured: with that block inside the
server, `a.css` came back as `application/octet-stream`. In production every
stylesheet, script, font and image would have gone out with the wrong type, and
a browser refuses CSS served that way. The site would have rendered unstyled on
its first deploy, and nothing in the repository would have said why.

Moved to the top level of the file, beside the `map`. A conf.d file is included
inside `http`, so there the block extends the map: `a.css` → `text/css`,
`b.md` → `text/markdown`.

**2. No charset on markdown.**

The files on disk are UTF-8; the header said only `text/markdown`, so a browser
fell back to its own default and Cyrillic arrived as `Ð‘Ñ�ÐºÐ°Ð¿`. Fixed with
`charset utf-8` plus a `charset_types` list that names `text/markdown` — nginx
charsets `text/html` unconditionally and nothing else unless it is listed.
`text/html` is deliberately absent from that list because including it only
produces a duplicate-type warning.

Verified end to end on a running nginx: css `text/css; charset=utf-8`, twin
`text/markdown; charset=utf-8`, `/about/` under `Accept: text/markdown`
`text/markdown; charset=utf-8`, under `Accept: text/html` `text/html;
charset=utf-8`, and Cyrillic round-tripping intact.

**Why nothing caught it.** `test/helpers.ts` serves the built site for the tests
and its own type map omitted the charset in exactly the same way, so a test
server more forgiving than production hid the bug it was meant to expose. It now
sends charsets too.

`test/nginx.test.ts` gates the config: the mapping exists, it is declared before
the server block, a charset is set, `charset_types` names markdown, and `Vary:
Accept` survives. Mutation-checked — reintroducing both faults fails exactly the
two relevant assertions.

Known and not fixable here: `astro preview` drops a prerendered endpoint's
headers, so a `.md` twin still looks like mojibake locally. Recorded in
CLAUDE.md, with the note that nginx over `dist` is what to check instead.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] A stylesheet is served as text/css by the shipped config, verified against a running nginx
- [x] A markdown twin is served as text/markdown with charset=utf-8
- [x] A negotiated directory address returns markdown with a charset under Accept: text/markdown
- [x] Cyrillic content round-trips through the server unchanged
- [x] The test server sends the same charsets production does
- [x] A test fails if the types block moves into the server block or the charset is dropped
- [x] The preview-server limitation is written down where someone will hit it

title: Phase 1d: ai-first tooling
description:
A typical agent arrives via one link, makes one request and leaves. It does not browse, does not see buttons, does not guess addresses. Priority follows from that.

1. Content negotiation on the same URL: Accept: text/markdown returns the agent version. Coding assistants already send that header, so it needs no cooperation. nginx map over two build trees; Vary: Accept is mandatory or caches will hand markdown to browsers.
2. Structured core (recipe) as the first block of an article, in both versions.
3. Twins at direct addresses: /<slug>.md, /<slug>.json, /index.json, /llms.txt, plus <link rel=alternate>.
4. Link header advertising llms.txt on every response.

R10: a build that does not emit all three outputs has failed.

Not doing: MCP or OpenAPI for readers — both require someone to wire up a client first.

Spec: docs/design/portal.md sections 6, 6a.

- [ ] Vary: Accept is present on every response — asserted in a test, because without it a cache hands markdown to a browser

title: Design the URL scheme, redirect map and frontmatter schema
description:
Precondition for all of phase 1.

1. URL scheme. Do not inherit Ghost's shape: articles sit at bare root there, so sections compete with slugs, and its slugs are transliterated Russian. New scheme: articles under /posts/<slug>/, plus /tag/, /about/, /projects/, /search/. Endpoints (/rss/, /llms.txt, /index.json, /webmentions/) are not content and take no language prefix.

/aboutme/ gets no special treatment: it is content, so it moves to /about/ and redirects like everything else. 'Already indexed' is true of every address here, and every address is being redirected anyway.

2. Language: prefixDefaultLocale false, per Astro's own recommendation. The default language has no prefix (/about/), additional ones do (/en/about/). An earlier draft argued for /ru/ from day one on the grounds that adding a segment later forces a second migration — that was wrong. With the default locale unprefixed there is no second migration either: Russian keeps its addresses and English, if it ever appears, arrives at /en/ without touching a single existing URL. Upside is real: shorter addresses for the language carrying all the traffic, and the framework's happy path instead of custom routing. lang stays authoritative in frontmatter, hreflang per page with x-default on the unprefixed tree.

3. Redirect mechanism. Astro's redirects config is NOT used. Its docs: astro build 'will output HTML files with the meta refresh tag by default' and 'if building to HTML files the status code is not used by the server'. Only supported adapters write real host config, and those exist for platforms ruled out on regional reachability. So the redirect map is a data file and a build step emits nginx configuration from it: one source of truth, real status codes, no dead meta-refresh pages.

4. Redirect map. Export every existing article URL and map it to its new address. 301 not 302, one hop only, never through an intermediate. Exhaustive — organic search is the only working distribution channel. /rss/ is the single exemption, for a mechanical reason: feed readers handle moved feeds unreliably and some drop the subscription silently.

5. Slug rewrite. Every address is being redirected anyway, so slugs are rewritten now: short, lowercase, readable, naming the subject rather than transliterating a headline. Free at migration time, expensive at any other.

6. CI test, two assertions per old address: the old one returns 301 with Location pointing at the new one, and the new one returns 200. Plus: no redirect target is itself a redirect.

7. Zod schema for Astro Content Collections: required (title, slug, date, kind, status, author, summary, tags, lang) and optional (aliases, updated, tools, sources, related, recipe).

Spec: docs/design/portal.md sections 3-5.
notes: 2026-09-08: redirect map DONE — migration/redirects.yaml, all 49 addresses covered one-to-one, verified against live sitemaps. Slugs, tag collapse (20 -> 6) and orphan-tag targets decided. Remaining in this issue: the Zod frontmatter schema, and the build step that turns redirects.yaml into nginx config plus the CI test asserting 301-then-200 with no chained targets.

URL scheme, redirect map and frontmatter schema all landed and are verified by checks a stranger can run.

Cross-field: updated cannot precede date, related cannot list the entry itself. 17 tests.

Exact-match 'location =' blocks, both slashed and unslashed form, 301 only. 14 tests, including that the committed conf is not stale.

title: Screenshot script, and the three things it caught
description:
The terminal redesign shipped twice without anyone looking at it, and both times
it was wrong in ways that a single screenshot would have shown in a second. Fixed
the cause first: `scripts/screenshot.ts` plus `npm run screenshot`.

On NixOS the browsers come from the nix store and its chromium build does not
match the revision the npm package expects, so `npx playwright install` is a trap
— it downloads a browser that will not start. The script resolves the binary out
of `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` and hands it to playwright directly, which skips
the revision check. CLAUDE.md carries that, along with two other things that cost
time this session: `preview` serves `dist` and shows nothing new until a rebuild,
and `verify` racing a running `dev` server dies on an unrelated filesystem error.

What the screenshots then showed, all three of them regressions from the identity
change (oh-my-portal-0zb):

1. `--frame: 62rem` put a path on the left and its date on the right with half a
   screen of nothing between them. They stopped reading as one row. Now 48rem —
   still wider than the reading column, so a status line still crosses the page.
2. The front page had no entry point: it opened on a line of small grey
   monospace. The heading was hidden behind `.sr-only` on the theory that the
   prompt line named the page. The highlight behind the heading was the thing
   worth removing; the heading was not. It is back, and `.sr-only` is gone.
3. The listing indented each summary by 2ch, the way `ls -R` indents. On screen
   that is a third left edge under a flush path and a flush title, and it reads
   as a mistake. Removed, and titles went from --step-1 to --step-2 so the page
   has something dark to land on.

Also: the `/` hint is hidden below 34rem, because a keyboard shortcut is worth
nothing to a thumb.

Verify with: npm ci && npm run verify   (0 type errors, 77 tests). test/search.test.ts builds the site, serves it, loads the built Pagefind index and searches it — Pagefind is a browser bundle but needs only fetch and WebAssembly, both of which Node has.

title: Status rail for /being.json
description:
The terminal frame (oh-my-portal-ve5) leaves room for a right rail and
deliberately ships without one: the being's state file does not exist yet, and a
panel fetching a file that is not there is exactly the fabricated telemetry that
every mockup in the design review was rejected for.

The shape agreed in that session:

- The being writes a small whitelisted JSON straight into the served directory —
  energy, count of live commitments, last activity. No commit, no rebuild, no
  deploy. §6a is untouched: nginx serving a file somebody else overwrites is not
  dynamic behaviour, so nothing moves into an application.
- The same file is the agent-facing artifact (§6), so one request serves both the
  human widget and somebody else's agent.
- The static HTML carries the last build's snapshot as the fallback, and the
  fetch replaces it. Without JS, and for an agent, a dated snapshot shows rather
  than an empty hole.
- Honest staleness: the rail says "тихо N дней" when the being is quiet. A cheerful
  state a month old is the lie this whole design is organised against.
- Whitelist, never blacklist: the being models its owner (user model, memories,
  message content). Only its reasoning *about itself* may be published. A
  blacklist eventually misses a field added six months later.

Blocked on oh-my-portal-dmb, which owns the inhabitant itself.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The rail renders from a snapshot in the built HTML and replaces it from /being.json when that fetch succeeds
- [ ] A missing, stale or malformed /being.json degrades to the dated snapshot, never to an error or an empty panel
- [ ] Quiet periods are stated in days rather than hidden
- [ ] The published field set is a whitelist, defined in one place, and carries nothing the being knows about its owner
- [ ] /being.json is reachable at its own address and documented in llms.txt

title: Commit hash in the article provenance line
description:

The one piece of provenance the reader cannot get anywhere else is the commit

--format=%h -- <file>` per entry, or one `git log --name-only` pass mapped to

checkout it does not own, and a shallow CI clone has no history to read.

- [ ] The lookup runs once per build, not once per article

title: Copy button and a code block wide enough to read
description:
Two faults the maintainer found by looking at the code article shipped in
oh-my-portal-zdu: no way to copy a block, and code clipped at the reading
measure so the end of a command was not visible.

**Code breaks out of the reading column.** Prose wants 34rem and code does not —
a command is one line whether or not it fits, and clipping it at the measure
hides the end of the thing a reader came for. A block now widens to `--frame` and
no further; below that width the expression collapses back to the column so
nothing overflows the page. Long lines still scroll, which is right for shell.

**Each block gets a header: the language on the left, a copy button on the
right.** A header rather than a floating button, because a button over the block
covers its first line, which in a shell block is the command. The language comes
from `data-language`, which Shiki already emits and nothing was using.

Both are built by script, for the same reason the search box is: the clipboard
needs JavaScript, and a button that cannot do its job is worse than no button.
Without JavaScript a block is still a block — selectable, scrollable, and
promising nothing.

The trap, and it cost a round trip: **article HTML arrives through `<slot />` and
the wrapper is created at runtime, so neither carries the component's scope
attribute.** Every scoped selector aimed at them matched nothing and failed
silently — a header the width of its own text over a block that never widened.
They all need `:global`, like the heading markers already did.

Verified with playwright against the running build: three blocks wrapped,
languages read as bash/yaml/bash, the clipboard contents equal the block text
exactly, and the button shows `скопировано` after the click.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] A code block is wider than the prose column and never wider than the frame
- [x] On a narrow screen the block collapses to the column and the page does not scroll sideways
- [x] Each block shows its language and a copy button
- [x] Clicking copy puts the block's exact text on the clipboard, verified by a browser, not by inspection
- [x] The button reports success, and reports failure honestly when the clipboard is refused
- [x] The button's text is kept out of the search index
- [x] With JavaScript off there is no button and the block still works
- [x] npm run verify passes

Widening a block to the frame bought a few characters and cost the page its left edge — prose starting in one place and every code block in another, on a site that is about reading. Reverted: blocks sit in the reading column like everything else, and long lines wrap with a hanging indent on Shiki's per-line spans, so a continuation reads as the same command rather than a second one. Two things had to be got right for that: pre { margin: 0 } inside the wrapper, or the browser default opened a white band between the header and the code; and white-space collapsing on the wrapper with pre-wrap on each line, because Shiki leaves a newline text node beside each line block and every block came out double-spaced. title: Split content into a private repository
description:
The engine stays public in oh-my-portal; articles move to a separate private repository.

Why: it turns the agent's permission boundary from a CI check we wrote into a credential the platform enforces — the agent's token reaches the content repository only and cannot touch templates, workflows, deploy settings or secrets. It also makes drafts private by construction rather than by discipline.

Work:
1. Create the private content repository with content/posts/, its own CI (build + deploy) and a deploy key.
2. Publish the engine as a git dependency: "oh-my-portal": "github:<owner>/oh-my-portal#<tag>". No npm publishing needed. Tag the engine; bumping the tag is the upgrade, and a broken engine commit cannot break publishing.
3. Issue the agent a token scoped to the content repository only.
4. Keep this repository free of real articles. Add a documented schema and two deliberately synthetic posts under examples/ so a visitor sees how content is shaped.
5. Keep engine issues in br here; content needs no tracker — a branch per article is the unit.

Cost to accept: the build needs two checkouts, and local engine work wants npm link.

Spec: docs/design/portal.md sections 2, 9.

title: Strip the shell to what the reference blogs actually do
description:
The maintainer rejected the terminal frame and pointed at github.com/letsila/awesome-blogs. Checked the markup rather than trusting memory: danluu.com ships 22KB of HTML and **no stylesheet at all**, opening straight into a dated list; eli.thegreenplace.net gives three links then a post; jvns.ca a name, a row of links and a sentence; brandur.org a name, nav and years. One shape: name → small nav → dated list of titles. Not one of them carries a status bar, a file path under a title, a reading time, tag counts, or a row of machine addresses. The page had all seven. Every value on it was real — that was the rule the whole terminal look depended on — and it was still too much: seven pieces of furniture around two articles, competing with the only thing a reader came for. Removed: the tmux status line and window numbers, the `$ ls ~/posts/` prompt, the `~/posts/.md` path on every row, the reading time, `проверено` in the listing, tag counts at the top, the `.md /index.json /llms.txt` footer row, and the visible `/` hint. The `/` key still works, unadvertised. The machine row deserves its own note, because removing it makes §6 honest again: an agent never renders this HTML. It arrives with `Accept: text/markdown`, reads `` in the head, or follows the `Link:` header nginx adds. A row of links to twins reached none of them and cost every human a line — the exact "billboard" §6 argues against, built anyway. Also changed: `автор человек` no longer prints on every article. A byline that reads identically for years is one readers stop seeing, which fails §8 in the other direction; the inhabitant's byline will be new when it appears. Caught by the screenshot loop while doing it: `
` inside `

title: Nobody has seen the site in a browser
description:
Two features are now built and asserted only structurally. Nothing about either has been seen working in a browser, because there is no browser on the build machine — no chromium, no firefox, and this is NixOS, where Playwright's prebuilt binaries do not run without extra work.

What is unverified:

1. The design system (section 12) — cream, the heading highlight, the pastel pills, the status-line footer, the reading measure. Selectors and markup are asserted; appearance is not. Phone width and desktop width both.
2. The /search/ page's DOM wiring. The Pagefind engine itself IS verified: test/search.test.ts runs the real engine against a real index and checks tool names, version strings and Russian queries. What is not verified is the page around it — the debounce, the out-of-order guard, result rendering, the ?q= deep link, and that the form actually appears when the script runs.

`npm run preview` serves a build with the Pagefind index in place, so search works there; `npm run dev` has no index and the page says so instead of failing.

Worth deciding rather than repeating: whether to add a headless browser to this repository's checks. It would turn both of the above into tests, and would be the only way the design system ever gets a regression test at all. The cost is a large binary dependency and NixOS packaging.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Someone has looked at /, an article, a tag page and /search/ at phone width and at desktop width
- [ ] A search typed into the box returns results, and /search/?q=wireguard works on load
- [ ] A decision is recorded on whether a headless browser joins the checks

2026-09-08: one obstacle removed. The dev and preview servers were binding to the IPv6 loopback alone, so http://127.0.0.1:4321 was refused while the printed URL said localhost and looked fine. Both now bind to 127.0.0.1 explicitly; HOST=0.0.0.0 reaches them from another machine. Verified over IPv4: dev, preview, the Pagefind index and a markdown twin all return 200.

Use npm run preview rather than npm run dev to look at search — the index only exists after a build.

title: Article page: top line, markdown markers, and a provenance page
description:
Applies the reference's article page. Three things landed, all of them facts the
build can compute rather than decoration.

**The top line, above the title.** Date, tag chips, and the twin's exact byte
length — the same three values the archive row carries, in the same order, so an
article and its line in the listing agree about what it is. `обновлено` and the
`author: being` byline moved below the title: neither is how a reader decides
whether to start.

**Headings carry their own markdown marker.** `##` before an h2, `###` before an
h3, generated by CSS so the marker can never disagree with the level. It is not
an ornament borrowed from the reference: §1 makes a markdown file the source of
truth and §6 serves that file at an address one click away, so showing the `##`
says what the page actually is.

**`/posts/<slug>/integrity/` — provenance for one article.** The sha256 of
exactly what `/posts/<slug>.md` serves, plus the commits that touched the file.
Both are checkable from outside the site, which is the only kind of claim worth
publishing about oneself:

    curl -s https://<site>/posts/<slug>.md | sha256sum

Verified against a running build: the page's hash and the served twin's hash
match, and the revision list renders from real `git log` output.

The hash is taken over `articleMarkdown()` rather than over the source file,
because the twin is what is published. History comes from git run in the file's
own directory — the engine builds against a content checkout it does not own
(§2). An empty history is a normal answer (shallow clone, tarball, uncommitted
file) and the page says so rather than inventing a row.

Also: prev/next at the end of an article, and the R10 twin for the new address,
without which check-outputs.ts would have failed the build.

Supersedes oh-my-portal-q6y, which asked for a commit hash in the provenance
line. A page is the better shape: the line stays short, and the full hash and the
whole history have somewhere to live.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] The top line shows date, tags and the twin size, above the title
- [x] h2 and h3 in article prose carry generated `##` / `###` markers
- [x] /posts/<slug>/integrity/ publishes the sha256 of the served twin and the file's commits
- [x] The published hash matches `curl <twin> | sha256sum` against a running build
- [x] A build with no git history renders a stated absence, not an invented row
- [x] The integrity address emits its markdown twin (R10) and check-outputs passes
- [x] An article links to its provenance page and to the articles either side of it
- [x] npm run verify passes

title: Terminal frame: status line, directory listing, provenance
description:
Applies the design agreed in the session that reviewed five mockups. The
synthesis: the terminal idiom supplies the **frame**, the existing §12 tokens
supply the palette, and prose keeps the text face.

What is taken from where:

- The tmux identity lives entirely in a **status line**, not in panes. Panes
  break R1 (every article is an address), the back button, and mobile, and a
  hand-written pane manager is exactly the code §12 says will rot.
- The archive becomes a **directory listing** — path, date, title, summary,
  state — instead of cards. No border, no radius, no shadow anywhere.
- A **provenance line** under the article title, built only from fields the
  schema already carries: date, updated, `recipe.verified_on`, author, tags.
- Reading time computed from the body word count. Real, not decorative.
- `/` focuses search, or goes to /search/ when the box is elsewhere. What makes
  a terminal feel like a terminal is that keys work.

Deliberately NOT done, and why:

- No right rail for the being's state. `/being.json` does not exist yet
  (oh-my-portal-dmb), and a panel fetching a file that is not there is exactly
  the fabricated telemetry every mockup was rejected for. The frame leaves room;
  the rail arrives with the data.
- No dark mode: oh-my-portal-ksx is still undecided and owns that call.
- No commit hash in the provenance line: it needs a build-time git read, which
  the engine does not do today. Filed separately.

Spec: docs/design/portal.md §8, §12.

title: Homepage quiet pass: fewer labels, one red, one rule language
description:
Design review of the homepage screenshot found the field-journal concept sound
but overloaded with devices: seven small monospace labels introducing sections,
red used for six different things, three kinds of separators, a full-width sunk
insert competing with the illustration, and interface-flavoured details
("Весь журнал · 5", leading zero in dates, code-like tag chips).

Plan, approved by the maintainer in chat on 2026-09-10, and done the same day:

1. Labels in Plex Sans, small and quiet; monospace only for data. "Открытый
   вопрос" label dropped (italic question carries itself); experiment label and
   stage share one line without a dot; topics labelled "Темы журнала".
2. Red is the author's hand only: observation bar, drawing annotations, revision
   underline. Theme control marks its choice in ink; observation label is quiet.
3. One pencil stroke, before the journal; rows, revision and footer use the
   straight hairline.
4. Revision insert sits on the page paper, aligned to the text edge, introduced
   by a straight rule and air.
5. Dates unpadded, "Весь журнал" without a count, tags as underlined words with
   a quiet count, listing kind unboxed.

§12 carries a "quiet pass" entry recording each cut and its reason. The label
count landed at five, not four: the experiment label is required by §12, the
observation needs its name, "Раньше/Теперь" are what make the comparison
readable, and the topics row is ambiguous without a heading.

title: Auto table of contents for long articles
description:
Not built. `render(post)` already returns `headings`, so the data is free — what
needs deciding is presentation and threshold.

The reference the maintainer picked puts a floating "к содержанию" control at the
edge of the viewport. That is a JS widget, and §12's maintenance principle says
what is built by hand is repaired by hand; a static block after the top line
costs nothing and rots never. Start there and add the floating version only if
the static one is actually found wanting.

Threshold matters more than styling: a table of contents over two headings is
noise. Below some count it should not render at all.

The twin gets one for free if it wants one — markdown headings already are an
outline — so this is a human-side feature only.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] An article with enough headings renders a contents list linking to them
- [ ] Below the threshold nothing renders, and the threshold is stated in the code with its reason
- [ ] Heading anchors are stable across builds so a link into a section keeps working
- [ ] It reads correctly on a phone

title: No story for images in content
description:
There is no image pipeline: nothing imports `astro:assets`, the frontmatter
schema has no `image()` field, and base.css styles a bare `img` and nothing else.
The maintainer wants to put pictures in posts.

§12's "no stock illustrations" is about decoration and does not forbid a diagram
or a screenshot inside an article — but the design doc says nothing about where
such a file lives, which is the actual question given the two-repository split
(§2): the engine has no content, so images arrive from the content repository
beside the markdown that references them.

The part that needs thought is the twin. An agent fetching `/posts/<slug>.md`
gets the raw markdown, so `![](./screenshot.png)` resolves against nothing on its
side. Either the projection rewrites image paths to absolute URLs, or the
convention is that authors write absolute paths and CI checks it — the first is
kinder, the second is simpler, and picking neither means the twins ship broken
links to precisely the readers §6 exists for.

Also to settle: whether images go through Astro's optimizer (a build-time cost
and a dependency on the file being importable) or are copied verbatim, and
whether alt text is required by the schema rather than by discipline.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] §4 says where an image file lives relative to the post that uses it
- [ ] An image referenced from a post renders in the HTML and resolves to a working absolute URL in the .md and .json twins
- [ ] A test covers the twin case, because a broken link there is invisible in a browser
- [ ] The alt-text rule is stated and enforced where it can be
- [ ] examples/posts carries one post with an image

title: Syntax highlighting has never been rendered once
description:
Neither example article contains a single fenced code block, so no build has ever
produced a highlighted block and nobody has looked at one. For a corpus about
homelab, kubernetes and security, a code block is the most-used element on the
site — and it is the one element the design has never seen.

What is actually there: astro.config.mjs sets no `markdown.shikiConfig`, so
Astro's default applies — Shiki with the `github-dark` theme, emitted as inline
styles on the element. On a near-white page that is a dark slab whose colours
come from nowhere in tokens.css and cannot be themed from it.

Design §12 says nothing about code at all, which is the root of it.

Decide and record: which theme (a light one, or a pair driven by the same tokens
as everything else), whether line numbers, whether a filename or language label
sits on the block, and how a long line behaves — the `pre { overflow-x: auto }`
in base.css handles it today, which is right, but it has never been tested with
real content.

The markdown twin is unaffected either way: it carries the raw fence, which is
what an agent wants.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] examples/posts carries a real article with fenced blocks in at least two languages, one with a long line
- [ ] A theme is chosen deliberately and configured in astro.config.mjs, not left at the default
- [ ] Code colours are legible on this page's ground and do not fight the tag palette
- [ ] The block has been looked at via npm run screenshot, on desktop and on a phone
- [ ] docs/design/portal.md §12 says what a code block looks like and why
